entry.title: Apple MacBook Pro M6 and iMac M6 Announced – 2nm Chip, ProRes RAW Media Engine, Up to 32GB Memory
entry.summary: Apple has brought its 2nm M6 chip to the 14-inch MacBook Pro and the 24-inch iMac. Both machines get two more CPU and GPU cores than before, Neural Accelerators in every GPU core, Wi-Fi 7 and a Media Engine with hardware ProRes and ProRes RAW support. For editors, the more import
entry.content:
Apple has brought its 2nm M6 chip to the 14-inch MacBook Pro and the 24-inch iMac. Both machines get two more CPU and GPU cores than before, Neural Accelerators in every GPU core, Wi-Fi 7 and a Media Engine with hardware ProRes and ProRes RAW support. For editors, the more important details sit further down the spec sheet: memory stops at 32GB, and the ports stay at Thunderbolt 4.

The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 starts at $1,999 and the iMac with M6 at $1,499. Pre-orders open tomorrow, October 28, and deliveries start on Friday, November 6. Both use the M6 chip that debuted in the Mac mini in August, which we covered in our Mac Studio and Mac mini launch article. In its full version, the M6 has a 12-core CPU (2 super cores, 4 performance cores and 6 efficiency cores), a 12-core GPU with a Neural Accelerator in each core, third-generation ray tracing, a Dual 16-core Neural Engine and up to 170GB/s of memory bandwidth. Unified memory starts at 16GB and goes up to 32GB. The Media Engine has one video decode engine, one video encode engine, one ProRes encode and decode engine and AV1 decode, with hardware acceleration for H.264, HEVC, ProRes and ProRes RAW. The entry-level iMac uses a 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU version of the chip.

The M6 chip and video work

Apple’s performance claims for the MacBook Pro compare it with the 14-inch M5 model: up to 30 percent faster graphics, up to 25 percent faster AI workloads such as LLM prompt processing, and a Neural Engine that is up to 1.9x faster. The application examples in the press release are Blender ray tracing (up to 1.3x faster than M5), Affinity image processing (up to 1.2x) and Xcode builds (up to 1.3x). For the iMac, Apple compares against the M4 generation and quotes up to 2x faster graphics and up to 5x faster on-device AI prompt processing in LM Studio. Apple also claims the M6 has the world’s fastest CPU core. None of the figures Apple published for these two machines involves a video editing or grading application, so for filmmakers the Media Engine and memory configuration say more than the percentages.

The Media Engine layout is the same as in the M5 Pro: one encoder, one decoder and one ProRes engine. The M5 Max doubles the encode and ProRes blocks. In practice, the M6 machines get hardware decoding for the formats most cameras record (H.264, HEVC, ProRes and ProRes RAW), but parallel exports, for example deliverables and proxies at the same time, share a single encoder. Formats outside that list, such as BRAW, R3D or ARRIRAW, rely on the CPU and GPU instead.

Memory is the more obvious ceiling. Both machines top out at 32GB, and on the MacBook Pro the 16GB base configuration runs at 153GB/s; the full 170GB/s needs 24GB or 32GB. For 4K timelines in Final Cut Pro, Premiere Pro or DaVinci Resolve, 32GB is workable. Heavy noise reduction, Fusion compositions or 8K material are where the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Pro (up to 64GB at 307GB/s) or M5 Max becomes the more realistic option. We covered those models in our MacBook Pro M5 Pro and M5 Max launch article.

MacBook Pro M6: XDR display, Thunderbolt 4

The 14.2-inch Liquid Retina XDR display carries over: 3024 x 1964 pixels at 254ppi, up to 1,000 nits sustained full-screen, 1,600 nits peak for HDR content, a 1,000,000:1 contrast ratio, P3 wide color and ProMotion up to 120Hz. For editors, the fixed refresh rates of 47.95, 48, 50, 59.94 and 60Hz match playback to the project frame rate, and the reference modes include HDR Video (P3-ST 2084). A nano-texture version of the display is optional.

On the ports side, the M6 model has three Thunderbolt 4 ports at up to 40Gb/s, plus HDMI, an SDXC card slot, MagSafe 3 and a headphone jack. The M5 Pro and M5 Max models have three Thunderbolt 5 ports at up to 120Gb/s instead. The M6 drives up to two external displays at 6K/60Hz or 4K/165Hz, or one display at 8K/60Hz, 5K/120Hz or 4K/240Hz. Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 are new.

Apple rates the 72.4Wh battery at up to 24 hours of video streaming and up to 16 hours of wireless web use, and says performance is the same on battery and on mains power. The laptop ships with a 70W USB-C adapter; with a 96W or higher adapter, it charges to 50 percent in 30 minutes. It measures 31.26 x 22.12 x 1.55cm / 12.31 x 8.71 x 0.61in and weighs 1.55kg / 3.4lb. Storage options are 1TB, 2TB or 4TB, and the colors are space black and silver.

iMac M6: two models, two different port layouts

The iMac comes in two versions, and the differences matter more for media work than the two extra cores suggest. The 10-core model has two Thunderbolt/USB 4 ports, supports one external display (up to 6K/60Hz), takes up to 24GB of memory and up to 1TB of storage, and has 2.5Gb Ethernet only as an option. The 12-core model has four Thunderbolt 4 ports, 2.5Gb Ethernet as standard, up to 32GB of memory, up to 2TB of storage, support for two external 6K displays (or one 8K/60Hz display) and an optional nano-texture glass. Both start with 16GB of memory and a 256GB SSD, which Apple says is up to 2x faster than in the M4 iMac. With 256GB, media has to live on external storage from day one.

The 24-inch (23.5-inch viewable) 4.5K Retina display has a resolution of 4480 x 2520 pixels at 218ppi, 500 nits of brightness and P3 wide color with support for 1 billion colors. It has no XDR or HDR mode and no ProMotion, so the iMac is an SDR editing screen. The iMac also has a 12MP Center Stage camera, a six-speaker system with Spatial Audio and Dolby Atmos support, and a three-mic array. It comes in blue, green, pink, yellow, purple, orange and silver, measures 54.7 x 46.1cm / 21.5 x 18.1in and weighs 4.42kg / 9.7lb (10-core) or 4.44kg / 9.8lb (12-core).

Both ship with macOS 27

Both computers ship with macOS 27 Golden Gate, which includes Siri AI and new Apple Intelligence features. For edit systems, the more relevant point is software support. In our macOS 27 article for video editors, Adobe and Apple had confirmed support, while Blackmagic Design and Avid had not listed macOS 27 as qualified. New Macs generally cannot run a macOS version older than the one they ship with, so anyone buying one of these machines for client work should check their NLE, plugins and I/O drivers first.

Where they fit

The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 is the entry point to Apple’s pro laptop line. It suits editors and shooters who cut 4K H.264, HEVC or ProRes, offload cards on location with the SDXC slot, and want an XDR display for HDR review away from the suite. Projects that need more than 32GB of memory, fast Thunderbolt 5 RAIDs or three external displays point to the M5 Pro version.

The iMac is an all-in-one for SDR work: proxy editing, assistant editor stations, social and YouTube production, and offices that need a clean setup. For that work, the 12-core model is the better fit, as it adds the two extra Thunderbolt ports, the second external display and Ethernet as standard.

Price and availability

The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 starts at $1,999 ($1,899 for education) with 16GB of memory and a 1TB SSD. In Germany, Apple lists it from €2,299 including VAT. The iMac with M6 starts at $1,499 for the 10-core model and $1,699 for the 12-core model ($1,449 and $1,599 for education), and at €1,799 and €1,999 including VAT in Germany. Pre-orders open on October 28 in 35 countries and regions, and deliveries and in-store availability start on November 6. B&H and CVP do not list the new models yet. More details are in Apple’s announcements for the MacBook Pro and the iMac, and on the MacBook Pro and iMac tech specs pages.

Would an M6 MacBook Pro or iMac cover your editing work, or do 32GB and Thunderbolt 4 push you to the M5 Pro? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: Apple Creator Studio Update Announced – MotionVFX in Final Cut Pro, Generate Fill, Cinematic Mode Encoding
entry.summary: Apple has announced what it calls its most exciting update to Apple Creator Studio since the subscription bundle launched in January. Final Cut Pro for Mac now ships with MotionVFX effects and plugins built in, the Content Hub adds stock video, and images move between Final Cut P
entry.content:
Apple has announced what it calls its most exciting update to Apple Creator Studio since the subscription bundle launched in January. Final Cut Pro for Mac now ships with MotionVFX effects and plugins built in, the Content Hub adds stock video, and images move between Final Cut Pro and Pixelmator Pro without reimporting. Let’s take a look at what changes for editors, motion designers and anyone handling sound in post.

The update arrives on the App Store in November as a free update for existing subscribers. In Final Cut Pro for Mac, MotionVFX templates, titles, transitions and graphics sit directly inside the app, together with tools for rotoscoping, tracking and color grading. The Content Hub, Apple’s library of curated stock assets, now includes video and is available inside Final Cut Pro. Editors can send any still image from the timeline to Pixelmator Pro and have the edited version update in the project automatically, and Pixelmator Pro adds Generate Fill for prompt-based image edits.

Final Cut Pro also gets more keyframe easing options, clips that can be disconnected from the primary storyline, and 23 new transcription languages. Motion adds MotionVFX plugins for color grading, 3D camera tracking and one-click selection, plus a new Displacement filter. Compressor can now encode Cinematic mode video from the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo. Logic Pro gets a redesigned Browser, a Stem Splitter that separates drums, and an intelligent assistant in beta. A subscription costs $12.99 / €12.99 per month or $129 / €129 per year.

We covered the launch of Apple Creator Studio in January, when Apple first bundled Final Cut Pro, Motion, Compressor, Logic Pro, MainStage and Pixelmator Pro into one subscription. In March, Apple acquired MotionVFX, the Polish developer best known for its Final Cut Pro plugins and templates, and this update is the first time that content appears inside Apple’s own apps. It also follows Final Cut Camera 2.4 and Final Cut Pro 12.4 in September, which added aperture control for the iPhone 18 Pro and Cinematic mode refocusing in post.

MotionVFX content inside Final Cut Pro

According to Apple, Final Cut Pro for Mac now gives editors access to “thousands of elements” from MotionVFX. These include themed templates, graphics, titles and transitions, as well as tools for rotoscoping, tracking and color grading. Until now, MotionVFX products were separate purchases from the developer’s own store. Apple does not list which individual MotionVFX plugins are included, and the press release does not say whether the one-time-purchase version of Final Cut Pro also receives this content.

The Content Hub is now available inside Final Cut Pro as well. It holds Apple-curated stock video, photos and backgrounds that editors can drop into a timeline to fill gaps or build quick mockups. Apple does not give the size of the video library or the license terms in the press release, so anyone planning to use these clips in client work should check the usage conditions first.

Final Cut Pro also adds generative image creation from text descriptions inside a project, with quick edits and style adjustments. Apple does not name the model behind it.

Workflow changes in the timeline

Apart from the new content, three changes concern day-to-day editing. Keyframe easing gets more options for finer control over animation curves. Connected clips can now be disconnected from the primary storyline and placed anywhere on the timeline, which addresses one of the long-standing habits that editors coming from track-based NLEs have had to adapt to in Final Cut Pro. Transcription adds 23 new languages, which extends caption creation and transcript-based search to more productions outside the English-speaking market.

Pixelmator Pro round trip and Generate Fill

The round trip between Final Cut Pro and Pixelmator Pro works for any image in the timeline. An editor opens the still in Pixelmator Pro, makes the changes, and the saved version replaces the original in the project with no reimport. Motion gets the same round trip, and Freeform follows in December.

Generate Fill is Pixelmator Pro’s new prompt-based editing tool. Users circle an area of the image and describe the change they want, or make a more precise selection with the existing Free Selection, Quick Selection and Magnetic Selection tools. According to Apple, Generate Fill matches the lighting, perspective and texture of the surrounding image, and the built-in Super Resolution feature upscales the generated content so it stays sharp at larger sizes. The result can be merged into an existing layer or placed on a new layer with a mask for further refinement. For editors, the obvious uses are cleaning up stills, extending backgrounds for title cards, or adapting a photo to a different aspect ratio.

Motion and Compressor

Motion receives its own set of built-in MotionVFX plugins, which Apple describes as tools for cinematic color grading, 3D camera tracking and one-click selection for visual effects. It also adds text-to-image generation and editing, the Pixelmator Pro round trip, the new keyframe easing options, a new Displacement filter and an interactive demo project for new users.

Compressor now encodes Cinematic mode video recorded on the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo. Together with the Cinematic mode editing that arrived in Final Cut Pro 12.4, this completes the path from capture to delivery for that footage inside Apple’s apps. Note that Cinematic mode editing in Final Cut Pro 12.4 requires macOS 27 Golden Gate, according to Apple’s release notes.

Logic Pro for sound in post

Logic Pro is primarily a music app, but several of the new features are relevant for editors who handle their own sound. The Stem Splitter can now isolate, replace or rebalance drum parts without the original multitracks, which helps when a licensed track needs a quieter rhythm section under dialogue. The redesigned Browser on Mac gathers loops, instruments and effect patches in one place. A feature Apple calls music understanding, an on-device audio analysis tool, classifies and tags added sounds automatically, so users can search their own collection or drag in a loop to find matching audio. Apple also includes a Splice library in the new Browser.

Logic Pro for Mac also gets a new intelligent assistant in beta, built on a combination of Apple’s own models and OpenAI. According to Apple, it can help with production workflows, start a new song, set up a vocal track from a single prompt, or refine an active project. On the iPhone side, Voice Memo Studio Sound reduces room ambience and background noise in recordings made on supported iPhone models, with the option to continue in Logic Pro. Logic Pro also gets a new interface design with Apple’s Liquid Glass look, and a Producer Pack from salsa producer Sergio George.

Keynote, Pages, Numbers and Freeform

The productivity apps receive an intelligent assistant in beta, also built on Apple models and OpenAI, that works with the content of the open document. Model Context Protocol (MCP) support lets external AI agents read content, make edits and run automated actions in Keynote, Pages and Numbers. Keynote adds the Keynote Interchange Format (.keyx), an open JSON-based file format. Stock video from the Content Hub and new templates and themes come to all three apps. Freeform adds text styles and board background colors.

Requirements and limitations

Several of the new features have restrictions that matter for a global audience. Both intelligent assistants are available in US English only. The Logic Pro assistant requires macOS 27 Golden Gate on a Mac that supports Apple Intelligence, and MCP support in Keynote, Pages and Numbers also requires macOS 27. We looked at how the major NLEs and plugin makers handle macOS 27 Golden Gate earlier this month.

The Creator Studio version of Final Cut Pro for Mac requires macOS 26.6 or later and runs on Intel and Apple silicon Macs, although Apple notes that some features require Apple silicon. Final Cut Pro for iPad requires iPadOS 26.6 or later and an iPad with an A16, A17 Pro or M1 chip or later. Logic Pro for Mac requires macOS 26.1 and Apple silicon. Motion and Compressor require macOS 15.6 or later. For Apple Immersive Video processing in Compressor, Apple specifies 32GB of RAM as the minimum and recommends 64GB with storage read speeds of 2,000MB/s or faster.

Price and availability

The update will be available on the App Store in November, free for existing subscribers. New subscribers pay $12.99 / €12.99 per month or $129 / €129 per year (euro prices from Apple Germany, including VAT), with a one-month free trial. Buyers of a new Mac or a qualifying iPad can get three months free. University students and educators pay $2.99 / €2.99 per month or $29.99 / €29 per year. Up to six family members can share the subscription through Family Sharing, and it is a universal purchase across Mac, iPad and iPhone. More details are on the Apple Creator Studio page and in Apple’s press release.

The one-time-purchase versions remain available on the Mac App Store: Final Cut Pro at $299.99, Logic Pro at $199.99, Pixelmator Pro, Motion and Compressor at $49.99 each, and MainStage at $29.99. The free versions of Keynote, Pages, Numbers and Freeform also continue.

Does built-in MotionVFX content change the value of the subscription for you, or will you stay with the one-time purchase of Final Cut Pro? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: Thypoch Simera-C 100mm T1.9 Announced – Telephoto Prime Completes Seven-Lens Cine Set
entry.summary: Thypoch has added a 100mm T1.9 to its compact Simera-C cine prime series, the seventh and final focal length in the full-frame set. The new lens takes the line beyond 75mm for the first time and targets close-ups, reaction shots , and narrative details. It keeps the familiar Sime
entry.content:
Thypoch has added a 100mm T1.9 to its compact Simera-C cine prime series, the seventh and final focal length in the full-frame set. The new lens takes the line beyond 75mm for the first time and targets close-ups, reaction shots, and narrative details. It keeps the familiar Simera-C formula of a 16-blade iris, 210° focus throw and native Sony E or Leica M mounts, at a price that stays well below traditional cinema glass.

The Thypoch Simera-C 100mm T1.9 covers the full-frame image circle (43.2mm) and uses an optical design of 11 elements in 8 groups. Its horizontal field of view on full frame is 21.4°, and the minimum focusing distance is 0.85m / 2ft 10in, measured from the sensor plane. The aperture runs from T1.9 to T16 through a 16-blade iris. Focus rotation is 210°, and both the focus and iris rings carry 0.8 MOD gears. The front diameter is 72mm / 2.83in, with an M67x0.75 filter thread. In Sony E mount, the lens measures 86.4mm / 3.4in and weighs 477g / 1.05lb; the Leica M version is 76.6mm / 3.02in long and weighs 451g / 0.99lb.

We first covered the series when the original four Simera-C cine lenses (28, 35, 50 and 75mm) arrived in 2024. Thypoch later added the 21mm T1.5 and, in May 2026, the 16mm T1.9 together with a six-lens kit. With the 100mm, the Simera-C family now spans 16, 21, 28, 35, 50, 75 and 100mm.

Optics and rendering

According to Thypoch, the 100mm is tuned for defined subject detail combined with soft, natural bokeh and smooth transitions into the out-of-focus areas. The company also highlights chromatic aberration control as a priority of the optical design.

Like the 16mm, the 100mm opens to T1.9, while the five focal lengths in between stay at T1.5. On a long lens with a 0.85m close focus, T1.9 already produces a very thin focus plane, and the lens has no electronic contacts, so focus pulling remains fully manual.

Matching the rest of the set

The 100mm shares its barrel length (86.4mm in E-mount) and its 67mm filter thread with the 75mm, and it is only 24g heavier. Gear positions are consistent across the series, so follow focus motors and screw-on filters can move between the two longest lenses without readjustment. Gimbal users get the same advantage: swapping between the 75mm and 100mm requires little or no rebalancing. For standard 80mm matte boxes, the 67-80mm adapter ring Thypoch recommends for the 75mm also fits the 100mm.

Mount options

The lens is available in black with a native Sony E or Leica M mount. With Thypoch’s positive-lock adapters, part of what the company calls its “M TO ALL” approach, the Leica M version can be used on compatible cameras from Sony, Canon, Fujifilm, Panasonic Lumix, and DJI. Each lens ships with front and rear caps, back-focus adjustment shims, a mount tool kit, and a warranty card.

Price and availability

Thypoch says shipping starts in late October 2026. The suggested retail price is $879 / €799 in Sony E-mount and $959 / €869 in Leica M mount (euro prices include VAT).

Is the 100mm the focal length that makes the Simera-C set complete for you, or would you rather see a longer lens or a zoom? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: SmallRig Cage and L-Shaped Plate for Sigma FP2 Introduced – Wooden Grip, HawkLock NATO Rail, Arca-Swiss Base
entry.summary: Although the Sigma FP2 hasn’t started shipping yet, SmallRig has its first accessories ready: a full cage with a built-in wooden grip and a lighter L-shaped mount plate. Both match the look of SmallRig’s original Sigma FP cage and are now available for pre-order. The new Sigma FP
entry.content:
Although the Sigma FP2 hasn’t started shipping yet, SmallRig has its first accessories ready: a full cage with a built-in wooden grip and a lighter L-shaped mount plate. Both match the look of SmallRig’s original Sigma FP cage and are now available for pre-order.

The new Sigma FP2 keeps the modular brick concept of the original fp: no built-in grip, no viewfinder, and accessories added as the job demands. That makes a cage almost mandatory for many video users. When the first fp arrived, SmallRig was quick with a cage for it as well, and the new FP2 cage follows the same recipe with a wooden handle on the right side.

The cage

SmallRig’s Cage for Sigma FP2 (item 6505) attaches with a three-point lock, combining a bottom screw, a locating pin and a side screw. According to SmallRig, this keeps the cage from twisting, while cutouts leave all buttons, ports and Sigma’s own accessories accessible.

For expansion, the cage has a built-in HawkLock NATO rail, 1/4″-20 threads and ARRI locating holes for magic arms, monitors and top handles. A modular cold shoe can be removed so that the cage stays compatible with Sigma’s original EVF. The base has an integrated Arca-type quick release plate, which SmallRig says mounts directly on Arca tripod heads and DJI RS 2, RS 3, RS 4 and RS 5 gimbals. An HDMI cable clamp is included to protect the camera’s port when an external monitor is connected, and a magnetic wrench is stored in the cage for tool-free adjustments.

The cage is made from aluminum alloy and stainless steel, with a wooden grip and silicone parts. It measures 127.8 x 53.0 x 89.6mm / 5.0 x 2.1 x 3.5in and weighs 174g / 6.1oz. In the box are the cage, the HDMI cable clamp, a cold shoe mount and a user manual.

The L-shaped mount plate

For users who want less bulk, SmallRig also offers an L-Shaped Mount Plate with Wooden Handle for Sigma FP2. It mounts with a 1/4″-20 screw and an anti-twist locating block, and protects the bottom and right side of the camera. A threaded hole on the back supports Sigma’s original optical viewfinder, and the bottom has 1/4″-20 threads and locating holes for Arca-type quick release plates. A magnetic wrench is integrated here as well. There is no NATO rail, cold shoe or HDMI clamp on the plate. It measures 125.0 × 56.7 × 79.0mm / 4.9 × 2.2 × 3.1in, and weighs 129.0 g / 4.6oz.

Price and availability

The SmallRig Cage for Sigma FP2 (6505) is listed at $79.99, and the L-Shaped Mount Plate at $49.99. Both are available for pre-order from SmallRig, with a 2-year warranty. The cage is expected to ship shortly before the camera, which Sigma will release on November 11, 2026 at $2,199 / €2,199 for the body.

For more information, please visit the SmallRig website.

Are you planning to rig up the Sigma FP2, and would you go for the full cage or the lighter L-plate? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: Sigma 50mm F1.4 CL DG Contemporary Announced – 375g All-Metal Prime, New RDD Autofocus, Intentional Softness
entry.summary: Sigma has announced the 50mm F1.4 CL DG | Contemporary, a compact full-frame prime that deliberately does not chase maximum sharpness. Its aberrations are tuned by simulation for a gentle softness in the focal plane, and a newly developed ring-shaped autofocus motor keeps the all
entry.content:
Sigma has announced the 50mm F1.4 CL DG | Contemporary, a compact full-frame prime that deliberately does not chase maximum sharpness. Its aberrations are tuned by simulation for a gentle softness in the focal plane, and a newly developed ring-shaped autofocus motor keeps the all-metal barrel short. It also starts a new “CL” lineage inside Sigma’s I series. But is a lens built for character also a good match for video?

The Sigma 50mm F1.4 CL DG | Contemporary is a full-frame mirrorless lens for L-Mount and Sony E-mount. It uses 9 elements in 6 groups (one FLD and three aspherical elements), a 14-blade rounded diaphragm and a new RDD (Rotary Direct Drive) autofocus actuator. The lens measures ø64.7 x 54.0mm / ø2.5 x 2.1in on L-Mount and ø64.7 x 56.0mm / ø2.5 x 2.2in on Sony E, weighs 375g / 13.2oz on both mounts and takes 52mm filters. It has an aperture ring, a distance scale with a depth-of-field scale, and a dust- and splash-resistant build. Sigma plans to launch the lens in early spring 2027. Pricing has not been announced yet.

A new branch of the I series

Sigma introduced the I series of “Premium Compact Primes” in late 2020, when three new Contemporary primes for L-Mount and Sony E joined the 45mm F2.8. The line grew over the following years, including the 50mm F2 DG DN Contemporary in 2023. All of these lenses share the all-metal body, knurled rings, aperture ring and magnetic metal lens cap. The CL keeps those elements and adds a second, faster 50mm to the series.

The CL is not a smaller version of the 50mm F1.4 DG DN | Art. The Art lens is designed for maximum resolution and weighs 670g / 23.6oz on L-Mount. The CL weighs 375g / 13.2oz and, according to Sigma, has a different design goal: its aberrations are “intentionally controlled” to give a soft rendering of texture in the in-focus plane, smooth bokeh, and a background that separates the subject. Sigma says the lens shows its best bokeh and three-dimensionality wide open at F1.4, and it names portraits and snapshots as the main uses.

The MTF charts on Sigma’s product page are for the lens wide open. Sigma also says that the placement of the aspherical elements suppresses ghosting, which it calls difficult to avoid in small, light lenses.

The RDD autofocus actuator

To keep the barrel short, Sigma uses whole-lens extension focusing instead of an inner focus design. This means that the motor must move a heavier focus group. For this, Sigma developed the RDD actuator. It uses the same coil-and-magnet principle as the company’s HLA (High-response Linear Actuator), but arranges the coils and magnets in a circle around the barrel. According to Sigma, this gives high torque without a large increase in lens diameter.

Because RDD drives the optics directly, the lens changes to manual focus temporarily when you turn the focus ring during autofocus operation. There is no AF/MF switch. The focus ring turns in direct sync with the focus movement, and the distance scale runs from the minimum focusing distance of 45cm / 17.8in to infinity. Maximum magnification is 1:6.8, and the minimum aperture is F16.

What it means for video shooters

Sigma presents the CL as a photo lens, and its marketing does not mention video. The B&H listing states that autofocus performance is slower than an STM or HLA system and that the lens is less suited to the demands of video autofocus. Sigma does not give data on focus breathing, and it does not say whether the front of the lens moves during focusing.

For manual focus work, the lens has more to offer. A focus ring with a printed distance scale that rotates in sync with the focus position gives repeatable marks for simple focus pulls. The 14-blade diaphragm keeps out-of-focus highlights round when stopped down. Sigma confirms an aperture ring, but it does not mention a de-click option. The soft rendering at F1.4 can also be a look for narrative and documentary work on small cameras, where a modern 50mm can be too clinical. Anyone who plans to use it on a gimbal or with continuous autofocus should first check how the focus mechanism behaves on their own camera.

For L-Mount filmmakers, the obvious pairing is Sigma’s own Sigma FP2, which was also just announced with 6K open gate and internal ProRes RAW. Sigma shot the official sample images for the CL on the 61MP Sigma fp L.

Build, mounts and accessories

The barrel, knurled hood, focus ring and aperture ring are made of metal. The lens has a dust- and splash-resistant structure, and the front element has a water- and oil-repellent coating. Sigma says that the lens is not waterproof.

The L-Mount version comes in black and silver. The Sony E-mount version is listed in black only. The box contains a pouch, the LH520-04B or LH520-04S lens hood (to match the finish), a LCF-52 IV front cap, a LCF52-02 MB or MS magnetic metal lens cap and a LCR III rear cap. The lens supports Sigma’s Mount Conversion Service, and the L-Mount version works with the Sigma USB Dock UD-11 (sold separately) for firmware updates. Like all Sigma lenses, it is made in Aizu, Japan.

Price and availability

Sigma has not announced a price for the 50mm F1.4 CL DG | Contemporary. The company plans to launch the lens in early spring 2027 for L-Mount and Sony E-mount, and Sigma America lists it as “In Development – Pricing and Availability TBD”. B&H already has a product page for the lens, with no price yet. CVP does not list the lens at the time of writing. For more information, visit the Sigma website.

Would you pick a 50mm that is designed to be soft wide open over a clinically sharp one, and would you use it for video? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.content:
GoPro has released two close-up filter options for the MISSION 1 and MISSION 1 PRO, made by PolarPro. The diopters slide over the camera’s fixed lens and give a closer focus range with a shallower depth of field. A single +0.5 filter costs $49.99, and a set of three strengths costs $99.99. But what do these filters change on a camera with a fixed 14mm lens?

The new GoPro Close-Up Filter is a single PolarPro +0.5 diopter. The Close-Up Filter Set adds +1 and +2 diopters and a travel case. According to GoPro, the filters use optical-grade, multi-coated glass and slide over the MISSION 1 or MISSION 1 PRO lens, or over an ND filter that is already on the camera. Focus is static, so there is no adjustment to make. Each strength has a fixed focus range: 50 to 150cm / 19.6 to 59in for the +0.5, 45 to 90cm / 17.7 to 35.4in for the +1, and 30 to 50cm / 11.8 to 19.6in for the +2. Both products are available now from GoPro.com.

The MISSION 1 series is GoPro’s line of large-sensor action cameras with a 1-inch 50MP sensor. We covered the MISSION 1 series announcement and, more recently, the free update with a zero-lag shutter and anamorphic support. This year, GoPro was sold to Starman Optical for $285 million, and Nick Woodman wrote after the merger that the cameras are staying. New accessories for the MISSION 1 line are one sign that this is the case.

Three strengths, three working distances

A diopter is a close-up lens: it moves the focus range of the camera nearer. On a fixed-lens camera with a 14mm lens, the subject must be close to get visible background blur. The diopter makes this possible because it moves the plane of focus close to the camera.

GoPro positions the +0.5 as an everyday filter for vlogs, lifestyle and travel footage. Its range starts at 50cm and ends at 150cm. GoPro’s footnote says that it limits the far focus distance to 150cm so that the filter can give subject separation. Thus, a background at a large distance stays out of focus, and this is the effect that GoPro wants.

The +1 gives a range of 45 to 90cm, and the +2 gives 30 to 50cm. With each step, the depth of field becomes shallower and the working distance becomes shorter. The +2 range of 30 to 50cm is a distance for tabletop shots, product shots and detail shots, not for a person who talks to the camera at arm’s length.

Stabilization and limits

GoPro gives one warning for the strongest filter. High-vibration activities and quick camera movements can affect video stabilization when the +2 diopter is on the camera. GoPro does not give more detail. A shallow focus range also means that a subject that moves out of the range goes soft, because the camera cannot refocus past the limits of the diopter.

The compatibility list names the MISSION 1, the MISSION 1 PRO and the MISSION 1 PRO bundles (Grip Edition, Creator Edition and Ultimate Creator Edition). The press release does not list the MISSION 1 PRO ILS, the model with a Micro Four Thirds mount. At NAB 2026, we gave the MISSION 1 PRO ILS one of our CineD Best of Show awards.

Price and availability

The GoPro Close-Up Filter (+0.5) costs $49.99, and the GoPro Close-Up Filter Set (+0.5, +1, +2) costs $99.99. Both are available now globally from GoPro.com and are covered by PolarPro’s Adventure Assurance program. GoPro Premium and Premium+ subscribers get 20% off, but according to GoPro, this subscriber price applies only when the subscription renews. The subscription is available only in some countries.

At the time of writing, B&H and CVP do not list the filters. GoPro has not published a euro price.

Would you use a diopter on a MISSION 1 for vlogs and detail shots, or is the fixed focus range too limiting for you? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: Riedel RefCam Referee Camera Enters the Deutsches Museum – 14 g Head-Mounted Unit From the World Cup Final
entry.summary: The Riedel RefCam is a 14 g head-mounted camera that clips into a football referee’s communication headset and sends a stabilized, wide-angle view of the match to the broadcast. It is the camera behind FIFA’s Referee View at the 2026 World Cup, and the unit worn at the final is n
entry.content:
The Riedel RefCam is a 14 g head-mounted camera that clips into a football referee’s communication headset and sends a stabilized, wide-angle view of the match to the broadcast. It is the camera behind FIFA’s Referee View at the 2026 World Cup, and the unit worn at the final is now a museum piece. Riedel Communications has handed it over to the Deutsches Museum in Munich, where it sits a few steps away from a 7 kg camera from 1839. There is some irony in the timing: a camera with a Riedel badge enters the museum only months after Thomas Riedel bought ARRI, one of the most iconic camera companies in the world.

The RefCam consists of a miniature POV camera on the referee’s headset and a small belt pack that records the footage or transmits it live over a private 5G network. Riedel developed it with two Bundesliga referees as a training tool, and it has since been used live in the Bundesliga, in handball and at FIFA tournaments. On October 21, Thomas Riedel officially handed the RefCam over to the Deutsches Museum. According to the museum, as reported by the German press agency dpa, the unit is the camera that referee Slavko Vinčić wore at eye level on his headset during the World Cup final in the USA, and it recorded Spain’s winning goal in the 106th minute from his point of view. The RefCam is on display in the museum’s “Foto und Film” (photography and film) exhibition, opposite a case with a Daguerre camera from 1839 that weighs 7 kg (15.4 lb). In its own announcement, Riedel adds that the RefCam will also be shown next to an ARRI camera. The RefCam product page lists the head-mounted camera at 14 g (0.5 oz), with electronic image stabilization and a wide-angle lens.

The ARRI camera beside it makes the display more interesting than a simple donation. Riedel Communications is not a camera company. The Wuppertal firm is known for intercoms, fiber networks and private 5G for live production, and the RefCam grew out of the headset it already supplied to referees. Yet in April, Thomas Riedel, founder and sole owner of the Riedel Group, acquired ARRI, a company whose cameras have been in museums for decades. He spoke with us about his plans for the Munich company in an exclusive NAB 2026 interview, together with ARRI Managing Directors Chris Richter and David Bermbach. Six months later, the first camera to enter the Deutsches Museum under his ownership is not an ALEXA. It is a 14 g unit with his own name on it, and it will stand next to an ARRI camera, with ARRI’s headquarters only a few kilometers away.

A camera built by referees

The RefCam did not start as a broadcast tool. Riedel developed it through a joint venture called In-YS (short for “In Your Shoes”) with the German Bundesliga referees Patrick Kessel and Nicolas Winter. The original idea was referee training: officials wanted to review matches from their own position on the pitch, to improve positioning and decision-making. Speaking at the 2025 IHF Men’s Club World Championship, Riedel’s Luca Marx described it as “a tool from referees, for referees”, according to the International Handball Federation.

The design priority follows from that origin. “When designing the RefCam, the main requirement was to build an extremely light camera that does not hinder referees in any way and still delivers excellent broadcast-quality images,” Thomas Riedel said at the handover (our translation from the German dpa report).

Inside the 14 g camera head

The system consists of a miniature POV camera that clips into the referee’s communication headset, plus a separate belt pack that either records locally or transmits the signal. According to the IHF, the camera outputs up to 1080p at 50 Hz and uses electronic image stabilization. An integrated microphone captures the sound on the pitch, and the referee can mute or switch it off. For the handball debut at the Men’s EHF EURO 2026, the announcement from Riedel and the EHF gave the weight of the complete system, camera and transmission belt pack together, as less than 150 g (5.3 oz).

Riedel sells the RefCam in two versions through its Managed Technology division, so customers book it as a service with Riedel engineers rather than buy a camera off the shelf. RefCam Record stores the footage locally for post-match review, training and content production. RefCam Live adds real-time transmission over Easy5G, Riedel’s private 5G network. At the friendly between Germany and Ghana in Stuttgart before the World Cup, an Easy5G core and two base stations carried the RefCam signal, which went to the TV production as SDI and joined a setup of approximately 30 cameras, according to Riedel. That match was the first time RefCam Live was used at an international football match.

From the Bundesliga to the World Cup

The camera’s first Bundesliga appearance came in March 2024, at a match between Eintracht Frankfurt and VfL Wolfsburg. Riedel used the record-only version, and the footage went into a 30-minute program, “Referees Mic’d up – Bundesliga”, that DFL Digital Sports distributed to national and international media partners, as described in Riedel’s press release. The IFAB (International Football Association Board) approved that use in coordination with the DFB, the DFL and the participating clubs.

FIFA tried referee cameras at the 2025 FIFA Club World Cup, and the IHF credits Riedel with that deployment. Pierluigi Collina, chairman of the FIFA Referees Committee, said afterwards that the cameras had gone “beyond our expectations”, as quoted by SVG Europe. In February 2026, the IFAB changed Law 5 of the Laws of the Game. Referee cameras, chest-mounted or head-mounted, are now a competition option, with the organizer supplying the cameras and controlling how the footage is used.

At the 2026 FIFA World Cup in Canada, Mexico and the USA, FIFA called the feature Referee View. According to FIFA, the camera was in use for all group stage games, and it recorded and transmitted HD video and audio in real time. Broadcasters cut it into live coverage and used it after the match, for goals, penalty decisions and long-distance shots. FIFA does not name the camera supplier in that statement. The museum’s account confirms that the camera on Vinčić’s headset at the final, played at MetLife Stadium on July 19, was the Riedel RefCam.

Stabilization in two stages

Footage from a running referee is difficult to use live, even with stabilization in the camera. For the World Cup, FIFA’s technology partner Lenovo added a second stage: an AI-based stabilization process running on servers at the International Broadcast Centre in Dallas. In its own description, Lenovo claims up to 60% less jitter and a 70% smoother camera path without a loss of sharpness, with an output of Full HD at 60 fps and a latency of approximately 3 seconds. These are manufacturer figures, and the delay is a practical point for live directors: the stabilized referee shot arrives several seconds after the other camera angles, which makes it more suitable for replays than for a live cut in a fast attack.

Broadcasters also limited how often they used the shot. Rob Levi, senior director at TNT Sports, told SVG Europe that the director cuts to the referee camera in live coverage only when the moment warrants it, and leaves it out when the game is too fast. Levi also recommended watching the clips with audio, because the sound shows how difficult the referee’s job is.

A perspective television never had

The technical limits matter less than the change in viewpoint. Football on television is watched from far away: the main camera sits high in the stands, and even the tight shots come from long telephoto lenses on the touchline. Both are the view of an observer. The RefCam puts the viewer at eye level in the middle of the pitch, at the speed of the game, with the sound of the players and the referee. A sprint to keep up with a counterattack, a crowd of players around a decision, or a handshake before kick-off look different from there.

We described a similar effect in our detailed look at the cameras of F1: The Movie. Formula 1 on television also comes from distant broadcast cameras, and the cars never look as fast as they are. The small custom cameras that Sony and Apple built into the cockpits for the film put the audience into the driver’s seat, and the sense of speed came from that position, not from higher resolution. The RefCam does the same for football, at 1080p and with a feed that still shakes at times. That imperfection works for it. A shaky, head-mounted frame reads as real, because it looks like what a person on the pitch would see, and the broadcast-quality cameras around it provide the clean coverage. The referee’s view is not a replacement for those angles. It is the one angle no other camera position in the stadium can give.

Beyond football

Riedel has taken the RefCam into other sports. At the 2025 IHF Men’s Club World Championship, three referee pairs wore it in the opening-day matches, the first time a referee camera was used at a major international handball event. The EHF then scheduled RefCam and Easy5G for the semi-finals and medal matches of the Men’s EHF EURO 2026 in Herning, Denmark, with the signal going live into the TV world feed. In basketball, Riedel deployed three RefCam Record units in December 2025 at a game in Germany’s 2. Basketball-Bundesliga, as part of a research project with the German Basketball Federation (DBB) and the German Sport University Cologne on referee decision-making.

Where to see the RefCam

The RefCam is now part of the collection of the Deutsches Museum in Munich, in the “Foto und Film” exhibition. “What personally fascinates me most is the miniaturization of camera technology, combined with the immense increase in image quality,” said Director General Michael Decker (our translation). The museum has documented the development of camera technology for 120 years, and Decker said the RefCam fits well into that history. Riedel does not sell the RefCam at retail. It is available as a managed service for leagues, federations and broadcasters. For more information, please visit the Riedel website.

Did the referee’s view pull you closer to the game during the World Cup, or do the shaky frames put you off? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

Featured image credit: Bundesliga referee Daniel Schlager wearing a Riedel RefCam. Image credit: Riedel Communications.

entry.title: Sigma FP2 Announced – 6K Open Gate, ProRes RAW, 24.5MP Partially Stacked Sensor
entry.summary: Seven years after the original fp, Sigma has introduced its successor. The Sigma FP2 keeps the brick-shaped, modular concept, but almost everything inside has changed: a new partially stacked full-frame sensor, 6K open gate recording, ProRes RAW instead of CinemaDNG, and a tiltin
entry.content:
Seven years after the original fp, Sigma has introduced its successor. The Sigma FP2 keeps the brick-shaped, modular concept, but almost everything inside has changed: a new partially stacked full-frame sensor, 6K open gate recording, ProRes RAW instead of CinemaDNG, and a tilting screen. Sigma again calls it the world’s smallest full-frame camera body. Here is what filmmakers need to know.

The Sigma FP2 is an L-Mount camera built around a 24.5MP partially stacked 35mm full-frame CMOS sensor (35.9 x 23.9mm). It records 6K open gate (3:2) video at up to 59.94fps, and Apple ProRes RAW HQ or ProRes RAW (12-bit) at up to 6K 29.97fps. H.264, H.265 and Leica’s L-Log are also available, and Sigma claims up to 14.1 stops of dynamic range in 4K full-frame L-Log. The camera has 70GB of internal storage in addition to an SD card slot and SSD recording over USB, 32-bit float audio with an optional accessory, phase-detection autofocus with subject detection, a tilting 3.15in touchscreen and a new BP-91 battery rated for about 130 minutes of video. The body measures 112.8 x 69.9 x 41.8mm / 4.4 x 2.8 x 1.6in and weighs 376g / 13.3oz without battery and card. The Sigma FP2 is priced at $2,199 / €2,199 for the body, and Sigma has set November 11, 2026 as the global release date.

From fp to FP2

Note the name: Sigma writes the new camera as “FP2” in capital letters, while the original Sigma fp from 2019 and the 61MP fp L from 2021 used lowercase letters. The concept stays the same. The FP2 is a small, flat body without a built-in viewfinder or grip, and users add a grip, viewfinder, hot shoe or cage as the job requires. A switch on the top plate toggles between STILL and CINE modes, and each mode has its own interface and settings.

Compared to the original fp, the FP2 is 3.5mm thinner (41.8mm against 45.3mm) at practically the same width and height. The body alone is 6g heavier at 376g. With battery and SD card, it weighs 460g / 16.2oz, against 422g for the fp. The FP2 keeps a dust and splash resistant construction, and Sigma builds it at its factory in Aizu, Japan.

The fp series has a loyal following among filmmakers, and the community has kept the original camera alive with firmware projects. Only a few weeks ago, we reported on an open gate hack for the Sigma fp that records 3K 3:2 CinemaDNG from the full sensor to an external SSD. The FP2 now does open gate officially, at 6K, with no hack required.

6K open gate and ProRes RAW

The headline video feature is 6K open gate recording, which uses the full 3:2 area of the sensor. Sigma positions this for productions that deliver in several aspect ratios, including vertical versions for social platforms. Video aspect ratios are 3:2, 16:9, 17:9 and 4:3.

Frame rates break down as follows. 6K records at 23.98, 24, 25, 29.97, 47.95, 48, 50 and 59.94fps, but electronic image stabilization (EIS) is not available in 6K. ProRes RAW HQ and ProRes RAW stop at 6K 29.97fps, so 6K above 30fps is limited to the compressed codecs. 4K offers the same frame rates up to 59.94fps, with 100 and 119.88fps in crop mode. 2K goes up to 119.88fps in 16:9 only.

The codec choice marks a clear change from the original fp. The fp recorded 8, 10 and 12-bit CinemaDNG internally, plus 12-bit RAW over HDMI to Atomos and Blackmagic recorders. CinemaDNG is not in the FP2 specification sheet. Instead, the camera records Apple ProRes RAW HQ and ProRes RAW internally. For log workflows, Sigma uses L-Log from Leica Camera AG, which is supported by most grading applications. A ProRes 422 option is not listed in Sigma’s specifications.

Recording media options are the internal 70GB memory, SDXC cards (UHS-II supported) and portable SSDs connected over USB 3.2 with bus power. Sigma says the internal storage supports high-speed writing and lets recording continue when the card is full. Continuous recording is limited to two hours.

What about dynamic range?

Sigma claims up to 14.1 stops of dynamic range when recording 4K full-frame L-Log. The company also states that the camera has seven stops of highlight headroom above middle grey at ISO 1250 and above. In Log and RAW, the FP2 has dual base ISOs of 1250 and 10000, with a range of ISO 1250 to 102400 (expandable down to ISO 320 and 640). In standard MOV recording, the base ISOs are 320 and 2500.

These figures are manufacturer claims, not measurements. For context, our lab measured about 11.3 stops (at SNR = 2) for the original fp in 12-bit CinemaDNG, and about 11 stops for the fp L in our lab test. Readers should keep the different methods in mind when they compare a spec sheet number with a lab result.

Rolling shutter and autofocus

The FP2 has an electronic shutter only, as the fp did. Sigma says that the partially stacked sensor has a high-speed readout that significantly reduces rolling shutter distortion, but it does not give a readout time. The original fp measured 20.8ms in UHD in our lab, and the fp L measured 21.7ms in full-frame 4K. Stills shutter speeds go from 1/25600 to 30 seconds, and the flash sync speed is 1/50 sec. (1/60 sec. in crop mode).

Autofocus is a big area of change. The fp relied on contrast detection, which was one of the main limits of the camera for run-and-gun work. The FP2 combines on-sensor phase detection with contrast detection, and subject tracking recognizes humans, dogs, cats and birds, with eye AF. Focus ring control can be set to linear or non-linear, which matters for manual pulls with modern autofocus lenses.

Audio, timecode and connections

Audio recording is now Linear PCM at up to 4 channels at 96kHz or 2 channels at 192kHz in 24-bit, or 32-bit float at the same channel and sample rate combinations. The fp recorded 2-channel 48kHz 16-bit audio. There is a catch for 32-bit float: it works only with the optional HU-21 hot shoe unit attached and the Panasonic DMW-XLR2 XLR adapter or the DMW-DMS1 shotgun microphone. The HU-21 uses the same hot shoe specification as OM System and Lumix cameras.

The 3.5mm microphone input doubles as a timecode input. There is no dedicated headphone jack on the body; headphone output goes through USB. The camera has two USB-C ports. Port 1 (USB 2.0) handles the EVF, audio, cable release and charging. Port 2 (USB 3.2) handles SSD recording, webcam (UVC) and audio (UAC) output, and charging. A full-size HDMI Type A port (version 2.1) completes the set. Sigma does not list RAW output over HDMI for the FP2.

Other features include Gyroflow support for stabilization in post, a webcam mode, waveform, histogram, zebras and false color, and settings that can be saved and loaded with a QR code.

Tilting screen and new viewfinders

The original fp had a fixed rear screen. The FP2 has a 3.15in touchscreen with about 2.1 million dots that tilts up by 90° and down by 45°, which helps with low-angle and high-angle work without an external monitor.

The new Electronic Viewfinder EVF-21 connects to the camera with a single USB-C connection and tilts upward by up to 90°. According to B&H’s launch text, it uses a 0.5in OLED panel with 5.76 million dots. Sigma also introduces the LCD Viewfinder LVF-21, which sits over the rear screen and gives an on-axis view.

The Director’s Viewfinder function is back and adds current cinema cameras. It simulates the frame of the ARRI ALEXA 35 Xtreme, ALEXA LF and Mini LF, ALEXA Mini, AMIRA and ARRICAM / ARRIFLEX, the Sony VENICE, VENICE 2 and BURANO, and RED cameras such as the V-RAPTOR XL [X] and KOMODO X. Anamorphic desqueeze is available at 1.25x, 1.3x, 1.33x, 1.5x, 1.6x, 1.65x, 1.8x and 2.0x. On the fp and fp L, Sigma added and extended this function through firmware, most recently with the fp and fp L firmware updates we covered in 2023. On the FP2, it is part of the camera from day one.

Battery, power and accessories

The new Li-ion Battery Pack BP-91 replaces the BP-51 of the fp series. Sigma rates it at about 370 still images or about 130 minutes of video, approximately 30% more than the original fp. The camera can also run on USB Power Delivery (Sigma recommends an adapter with 27W or more) or on the new DC Connector CN-91.

Sigma lists these optional accessories: Hand Grip HG-11, Electronic Viewfinder EVF-21, LCD Viewfinder LVF-21, Base Plate BPL-21, Hot Shoe Unit HU-21, Cable Release CR-51, Battery Charger BC-91 and DC Connector CN-91. Note that the hot shoe unit is now an optional accessory. A pouch, battery, strap and SH-11 strap holder are in the box.

Stills and color modes

For photographers, the FP2 shoots 14-bit lossless compressed DNG and JPEG at 6016 x 4012 pixels, with continuous shooting at up to 20fps for up to 200 JPEG or 180 DNG frames. Stills base ISOs are 320 and 2500, with a range of ISO 100 to 102400 (expandable down to ISO 6). There is no in-body stabilization; EIS is available for video only.

A dedicated Color button gives access to 13 color modes: Standard, Rich, Calm, Powder Blue, Warm Gold, Teal and Orange, FOV Classic Blue, FOV Classic Yellow, Forest Green, Sunset Red, Cinema, 709 Look and Monochrome. Several of them come from the fp series. Sigma says the 709 Look mode is based on the Rec.709 standard and gives natural, understated tones, which can be useful as a baked-in look for fast turnaround work.

Price and availability

The Sigma FP2 body costs $2,199 at B&H. B&H also takes pre-orders for the kit with the EVF-21 viewfinder at $2,749, with an estimated ship date of November 11. Sigma also offers a kit with the 50mm F2 DG Contemporary lens. In Europe, Sigma Germany lists the body at €2,199 including VAT. CVP takes pre-orders for the FP2 kits with the EVF-21 and with the 50mm F2 lens. Sigma has set Thursday, November 11, 2026 as the global release date.

For comparison, the original fp launched at $1,899, and the fp L costs $2,499 at B&H. At $2,199, the FP2 adds 6K open gate, ProRes RAW, phase-detection AF and a tilting screen for $300 more than the fp did at launch. For more details, see the Sigma FP2 product page.

Is the FP2 the compact full-frame cinema camera that fp owners were waiting for, or do you miss CinemaDNG? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: Schneider-Kreuznach Nano Clear Filter Announced – Improved Color Neutrality, Broadband Anti-Reflection Coating
entry.summary: Schneider-Kreuznach has introduced Nano Clear, the next generation of its Clear protection filter for cinema lenses. A protection filter has one task beyond protecting the lens: to have as little effect on the image as possible. With a new broadband anti-reflection nano coating,
entry.content:
Schneider-Kreuznach has introduced Nano Clear, the next generation of its Clear protection filter for cinema lenses. A protection filter has one task beyond protecting the lens: to have as little effect on the image as possible. With a new broadband anti-reflection nano coating, Schneider-Kreuznach says Nano Clear reduces reflections and brings the filter’s color point very close to D65. The price is expected to remain the same as the Clear filter it replaces. The company announced Nano Clear on October 16, 2026, and showed it for the first time at CineVerse Roma at Cinecittà Studios.

Schneider-Kreuznach has a long history in cinema filters, and we have covered several of its products over the years. Nano Clear sits at the more straightforward end of their lineup, but for cinematographers who regularly work with protective filters, optical neutrality is the whole point. A clear filter protects the front element or other filters from dirt, moisture, and accidental damage. The tradeoff is that any additional glass in the optical path can introduce reflections, reduce contrast, or affect color. For a protection filter, the goal is therefore simple: protect the lens while changing the image as little as possible.

Available in two standard cinema filter sizes

The Schneider-Kreuznach Nano Clear is a 4mm thick glass plate in the two common matte box formats: 4 x 5.65in (101.6 x 143.5mm) and 6.6 x 6.6in (167.6 x 167.6mm). The 4mm thickness is unchanged from the existing Clear filter. The 4 x 5.65in version weighs 7.0oz (199.6g), and the 6.6 x 6.6in version weighs 13.3oz (376.5g).

Fewer reflections, same exposure

The main change is a new coating upgrade that Schneider-Kreuznach calls Broadband Anti-Reflection Nano Coating, which minimizes reflections and gives very neutral color reproduction with “virtually no visible color shift.” Resolution, contrast, and sharpness stay the same, and you don’t need to change any camera settings when the filter is in place.

How neutral is “neutral”?

Schneider-Kreuznach says that independent measurements place the Nano Clear very close to the D65 reference point. The Nano Clear fact sheet shows both the Nano Clear and previous Clear filter inside a MacAdam ellipse, which represents a range of chromaticity differences that are difficult for the human eye to distinguish. The Nano Clear point sits closer to D65 than the previous Clear filter, and on a multi-camera job where one camera carries a clear filter and another does not, even a small color shift can mean more work in the grade.

Easier to clean

The nano coating has one more function: it repels water. The surface also repels dust and dirt, so cleaning is faster in difficult conditions. For a protection filter, this is a practical improvement. Rain and spray are the conditions a clear filter is meant to handle, and water droplets that bead and run off are easier to deal with between takes than a film of water on the glass. Schneider-Kreuznach lists the key features as follows:

  • Protection for lenses and filter systems
  • Improved color neutrality with virtually no color shift
  • Broadband anti-reflection nano coating
  • Water-repellent surface for easy cleaning
  • No loss of resolution, contrast, and sharpness
  • No camera setting changes necessary

Price and availability

Schneider-Kreuznach says the Nano Clear is priced the same as the Clear filter it replaces. For reference, B&H sells the current Schneider Clear filter for $253.80 in 4 x 5.65in and $405 in 6.6 x 6.6in. Shipping is expected to start at the end of November 2026. For more information, visit the Schneider-Kreuznach website.

Do you keep a clear filter on your lenses all the time, or only when the conditions are rough? Let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: Your Shot – Free Super Slow Motion Tennis Event in Vienna with Pixboom Spark Tomorrow, No Registration
entry.summary: Tomorrow, Friday October 23, anyone in Vienna, Austria, can step onto a tennis court, hit a ball, and walk away with a cinematic super slow motion clip of themselves, captured by a camera robot at up to 1,000 frames per second. It is free, there is no registration, and you just s
entry.content:
Tomorrow, Friday October 23, anyone in Vienna, Austria, can step onto a tennis court, hit a ball, and walk away with a cinematic super slow motion clip of themselves, captured by a camera robot at up to 1,000 frames per second. It is free, there is no registration, and you just stop by.

We are calling it Your Shot, and the idea is simple. Red carpet events have the Glambot, that robotic arm that swings past celebrities and turns a half-second pose into a dreamy slow motion moment. We built one for tennis – and call it Grand Slambot. On Friday, from 1 to 5pm, a Bolt Jr high-speed camera robot carrying a Pixboom Spark will be waiting at the Wiener Athletiksport Club in the Prater.

How it works

You show up, you get a racket in your hand, and you hit a ball while the Grand Slambot sweeps past you in a repeatable, pre-programmed move. The Spark records the moment at roughly 1,000 frames per second, which stretches a split second of impact into several seconds of footage: the ball compressing on the strings, the racket flexing, your face doing whatever faces do at the moment of contact. Afterwards, you receive a QR code, and once the clip is processed you download it and share it wherever you like.

No tennis skills are required. The robot does the hard part, and a slightly awkward swing in super slow motion looks at least as good as a perfect one. Children and adults are both welcome, and if you are a member of the club, bring your friends.

Why we are doing this

Your Shot is part of a bigger project. CineD and MZed are producing a free course on high-speed filmmaking in partnership with Pixboom, the company behind the Spark, and Friday doubles as the shoot for the lesson on sports and motion control. Our production partner MXR Productions turns the court into a real set for the day: the Bolt Jr with its own motion control operator, a camera crane, an ARRI ALEXA 35 for the behind-the-scenes, and proper lighting. In other words, this is a working high-speed production that you get to walk into and take part in.

For us, the day answers a question we have been circling for months. Cameras like the Spark have moved cinema-grade slow motion from six-figure rental packages to something a small crew can set up on a tennis court, and we wanted to show what that looks like in practice rather than on a spec sheet. We tested a beta unit of the camera earlier this year, and Friday is the first time we put the production version to work in front of an audience.

By taking part, you agree that the footage may appear in the course and in the campaign around it. Your own clip is yours to keep and share.

When and where

Friday, October 23, from 1 to 5pm, at the Wiener Athletiksport Club (WAC), Rustenschacherallee 9, 1020 Vienna, a short walk from the Prater Hauptallee. Entry is free and no registration is needed, just come by during the afternoon. For more information on the camera, please visit the Pixboom website.
