entry.title: Cooke S4 FF/i Announced – Full-Frame T2.0 Primes, 385mm Average Close Focus, 87mm Front Diameter
entry.summary: Cooke Optics has introduced the S4 FF/i, a full-frame evolution of its S4/i Super 35 primes. The set has six T2.0 lenses from 18mm to 100mm, a common 87mm front diameter and close focus that averages just over 15 inches. With the original S4/i out of production since the start of
entry.content:
Cooke Optics has introduced the S4 FF/i, a full-frame evolution of its S4/i Super 35 primes. The set has six T2.0 lenses from 18mm to 100mm, a common 87mm front diameter and close focus that averages just over 15 inches. With the original S4/i out of production since the start of 2025, the new series puts the S4 name back into Cooke’s PL and LPL lineup.

The Cooke S4 FF/i range includes 18mm, 25mm, 35mm, 50mm, 75mm and 100mm focal lengths, all at T2 to T16. Each lens comes in PL or LPL mount, has a nine-blade iris with curved blades and carries Cooke’s latest /i Technology for lens metadata. The lenses weigh between 1.45kg / 3.2lbs and 1.8kg / 4.0lbs with a PL mount. The front diameter is 87mm / 3.42in on every focal length, and all lenses except the 18mm accept M82 x 0.75 screw-in filters. In the UK, CVP lists the lenses at £11,000 ex VAT each. We reported in December 2024 that Cooke S4 and S4/i lenses would be discontinued, with production ending on January 1, 2025. The S4 FF/i is not a rehoused S4/i. Cooke describes it as a new lens design that keeps some optical qualities of the Super 35 set and updates them for full-frame cameras.

The S4 FF/i joins Cooke’s other full-frame spherical lines, which include the faster S8/i FF T1.4 primes and the vintage-styled Panchro/i Classic FF range. For mirrorless mounts, the company recently brought its SP3 and AP3 lenses to Nikon Z mount. Cooke calls the S4 FF/i “the everyday set”, and positions it as a compact workhorse for handheld, gimbal and Steadicam work.

Six focal lengths, one front diameter

Cooke’s specification sheet gives the following figures with a PL mount. The 18mm is 124mm / 5.07in long and weighs 1.8kg / 4.0lbs. The 25mm is 110mm / 4.33in long and weighs 1.65kg / 3.6lbs. The 35mm is 107.5mm / 4.23in long and weighs 1.7kg / 3.75lbs.

The 50mm is the lightest lens in the set at 1.45kg / 3.2lbs, with a length of 94.6mm / 3.72in. The 75mm is the shortest at 89.3mm / 3.51in and weighs 1.6kg / 3.5lbs. The 100mm is 106.6mm / 4.19in long and weighs 1.65kg / 3.65lbs. Length is measured from the front of the lens to the lens mount.

The average weight across the set is 1,642g. According to Cooke, the lenses are 29% lighter on average than the original S4/i S35 primes, and the company calls the set “among the lightest and most compact cinema lens sets Cooke has ever delivered.” A common 87mm front diameter means one clamp-on matte box size fits the whole set. Focus gears have 123 teeth and iris gears have 117 teeth, both at 0.8 metric module. The focus scale turns 270° from infinity to the minimum marked distance, and the iris scale turns 75°.

What about close focus?

Close focus is one of the main points that Cooke makes about the S4 FF/i. Measured from the sensor, the minimum marked object distance is 300mm / 12in on the 18mm, 280mm / 11in on the 25mm and 35mm, 350mm / 14in on the 50mm, 450mm / 18in on the 75mm and 650mm / 2ft 3in on the 100mm. Cooke gives the average as 385mm, or just over 15 inches.

The specification sheet also lists close focus from the front of the lens, which is the more useful figure for working distance on set. The values are 124mm / 5.07in for the 18mm, 118mm / 4.62in for the 25mm, 121mm / 4.72in for the 35mm, 203mm / 8.23in for the 50mm, 309mm / 12.44in for the 75mm and 491mm / 20.76in for the 100mm. Cooke says that hands and small details can fill the frame, and that performance holds from infinity to the minimum object distance. Focus scales are available in imperial or metric, marked from infinity to MOD.

Coverage and angle of view

The lenses cover full frame, and Cooke names the RED V-RAPTOR, Sony VENICE and ARRI ALEXA LF as target cameras. The specification sheet uses a 36 x 24mm format with a 43.27mm diagonal for its full-frame angle of view figures. Cooke does not publish a separate image circle figure.

On full frame, the maximum diagonal angles of view are 101.9° (18mm), 83.6° (25mm), 63.4° (35mm), 46.7° (50mm), 32.2° (75mm) and 24.4° (100mm). On a Super 35 format with a 30mm diagonal, the figures are 82.2°, 65.4°, 48.3°, 34.7°, 23.5° and 17.8°.

The look: flares, skin tones and bokeh

Cooke says the S4 FF/i keeps the natural skin tones of the S4/i S35, with “a gentleness to faces akin to a very light filtration.” The company describes detail as having “gentle clarity rather than a brittle or clinical edge,” and says the lenses add a slight warmth to the image. Highlights have a slight glow and bloom, according to Cooke.

Flares are layered, and veiling flare takes on the color of the light source. Cooke states that each focal length flares a little differently. Contrast softens in flare without the picture becoming hazy, according to the company.

Cooke also says that sharpness holds from edge to edge with very little loss of detail towards the corners, and that contrast falloff is gentle. Bokeh is circular wide open and takes on a cat’s eye shape towards the frame edges, and Cooke says that this change is consistent across the focal lengths. The S4/i S35 had an iris with eight straight blades. The new nine-blade iris with curved blades keeps out-of-focus highlights rounder when the lens is stopped down. The iris has two opposing linear T-scales, with whole and third stops marked. All lenses in the series are color matched.

/i Technology and metadata

Each S4 FF/i lens has Cooke’s latest /i Technology. Data goes through the lens mount contacts and a cable connector. The real-time data includes focus position, iris position and inertial motion data. Every lens also has its own factory-calibrated shading and distortion map, which it transmits with the other data.

These maps are used by the Cooke Digital Lens System, a set of Nuke nodes that uses per-frame metadata and individually measured lens profiles for distortion management in camera tracking, matchmove and compositing. Cooke also notes the benefits for virtual production. According to Cooke, more than 300 lens models from different manufacturers support /i Technology, and major cinema cameras record the metadata directly into their RAW files.

Build and service

The lenses are handmade at Cooke’s factory in Leicester, UK. Each lens has a scratch-resistant coating on its exterior. Cooke says that the lenses are designed for easy servicing and maintenance, to keep downtime to a minimum.

David Hancock, CEO of Cooke Optics, said: “This lens series is the result of years of planning and work by my dedicated colleagues. I hope this lens can continue Cooke’s core purpose: a tool to empower a diverse variety of artists to express a wide array of distinctive, emotion-based visual storytelling.”

Price and availability

In the UK, CVP lists the Cooke S4 FF/i lenses at £11,000 ex VAT each (about £13,200 including 20% VAT), with PL and LPL versions at the same price. The complete six-lens PL set costs £66,000 ex VAT (£79,200 including VAT). CVP lists the single lenses as special order items and the set as available for backorder. At the time of writing, B&H does not list the S4 FF/i, and Cooke has not published a US dollar price. Cooke has not announced a shipping date. Its Rent or Buy page lists resellers and rental houses. For more information, please visit the Cooke website, where you can also download the full specification sheet.

Did you shoot with the original S4/i, and would a lighter full-frame version bring you back to the set? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: cinemaOS, CUTROOM, and invideo Compared – Mac Studio App, Free Open-Source Editor, Cloud AI Agent
entry.summary: A growing number of video editors are now built around AI and open-source components, some of them by small teams or a single developer. Three current examples take very different routes: cinemaOS is a Mac subscription app with an on-device assistant, CUTROOM is a free open-sourc
entry.content:
A growing number of video editors are now built around AI and open-source components, some of them by small teams or a single developer. Three current examples take very different routes: cinemaOS is a Mac subscription app with an on-device assistant, CUTROOM is a free open-source editor that runs locally, and invideo puts an AI editing agent and dozens of generative models in the browser. We look at each platform and then compare them.

The three products target overlapping users but differ in where the software runs, how AI is used, and how users pay. cinemaOS from Momentum Studios is a Mac-native application for Apple Silicon that combines editing, color, sound, design, and delivery for $9.99 per month. CUTROOM is a free desktop editor under the MIT license, currently in a 1.2 public beta for Windows and Mac, with optional local or bring-your-own-key AI. invideo is a web-based “agentic video editor” with mobile apps, sold in credit-based plans that start at $10 per seat per month on annual billing.

We have previously reported on ArtCraft’s free, open-source Adobe alternatives, which developer Brandon Thomas says he wrote with the help of an AI coding model, and on Adobe’s settlement with the US Department of Justice over its subscription practices. The established editors are adding AI as well, as we covered with DaVinci Resolve 21.1 and the new color tools and Firefly models in Premiere.

cinemaOS: one Mac app for every room

cinemaOS is made by Momentum Studios BV, founded by Julien Hayet-Kerknawi, and is currently at version 0.2 (build 9). The application divides work into “rooms” that share one live project. The Sequencer is a multitrack timeline for picture and sound that imports XML or EDL, exports FCPXML or EDL, and supports cutting from a transcript. The Finisher covers color grading with scopes and Shot Match, a 16:9-to-9:16 reframe function that tracks the main subject, plus subtitles, translation, and delivery. Atelier handles posters, photos and brand kits, and a Sound mode called Spatial Theatrics shows the mix as a 3D theater in which tracks become objects, with DX, MX, FX, and AMB buses and scene loudness measured against a target.

The built-in assistant, J.A.R.E.D., takes plain-language requests via Command-J. According to Momentum Studios, transcription, translation, and looks run on the Mac, need no credits, and subtitles can be translated with Wi-Fi off. The company does not name the AI models, and it does not publish supported codecs, RAW formats, or a minimum macOS version.

CUTROOM: free, open source and local

CUTROOM is published on GitHub under the account of Vano Peradze, and the website names no company. It is a desktop editor in a 1.2 public beta for Windows and for macOS 15 or later on Apple Silicon or Intel. Linux users can run it from source, without a packaged download. Setup installs Python 3.12 and media dependencies, and the Mac version uses FFmpeg 7 through Homebrew. The project states that the Mac build is not a signed app.

CUTROOM offers six workspaces: Media, Edit, Layout, Audio, Captions, and Output. Editing covers independent tracks, cuts, trims, and track locks; Layout adds crop and picture-in-picture for camera and screen recordings, and the audio mixer has live meters, mute, and solo. Captions can be imported as SRT or VTT. Export is MP4 in landscape or vertical, up to 4K and 60fps, without a watermark. AI is optional: manual editing needs no models or account, local transcription and drafts use downloadable models and Ollama, and users can connect their own API key for a cloud provider, which then charges them directly. The project itself notes that AI drafts “may miss context or have weak endings.”

invideo: an AI agent in the browser

invideo calls its product “the agentic video editor for serious creatives.” The workflow is to upload footage, describe the edit to the Agent Two assistant, review the cut, and export. According to the company, the agent watches and logs every clip, and users can take over the multitrack timeline at any frame. Custom agents carry roles such as scriptwriter, editor, cinematographer, sound designer, and colorist, and invideo lists multiplayer editing, storyboarding, and the option to connect outside agents such as Claude Cowork, ChatGPT Codex, Grok, and Gemini.

The other major part of invideo is generative media. The site lists video models including Google Veo 3.1, Sora 2, Kling, Wan, Pixverse, Hailuo and Seedance, image models such as Nano Banana Pro, Ideogram, Seedream and Flux Kontext, and audio from ElevenLabs and MiniMax. Generations use monthly credits that do not roll over, and invideo states that it can change credit costs without notice. Plans include 4K export of the user’s own footage, storage from 200GB to 2,000GB, and premium stock footage. invideo runs in the browser, with iOS and Android apps.

Where the work runs

The clearest difference between the three is the location of media and processing. cinemaOS keeps projects, media, and versions on the user’s disk and runs its assistant on the Mac. CUTROOM also edits, previews, and exports locally, and it sends audio or transcripts to a cloud provider only when the user connects one and gives consent. invideo is a cloud service: footage is uploaded, and the agent and generative models run on invideo’s side. For productions with confidentiality requirements, that difference may matter more than the feature lists.

AI as assistant or as editor

The role of AI also differs. In cinemaOS, J.A.R.E.D. carries out looks, transcription, and translation on request inside a conventional editing application. CUTROOM treats AI as an option for transcripts and first drafts, with the timeline remaining manual. invideo puts the agent at the center of the workflow and adds generation of new shots, images, voices and music, which the other two do not offer.

Platforms, formats and maturity

cinemaOS is Mac only until a Windows version arrives in November 2027, according to the company. CUTROOM supports Windows and Mac now, while invideo works in any browser and on phones. On interchange, only cinemaOS lists XML, EDL, and FCPXML, which gives a path to and from other editors; CUTROOM documents MP4 output and SRT or VTT captions, and invideo does not list project interchange formats on its main pages. Both cinemaOS (version 0.2) and CUTROOM (public beta) are early releases, and CUTROOM’s own page lists acceptance testing that is still pending.

A threat to Premiere Pro, Final Cut Pro and DaVinci Resolve?

On the evidence of their own documentation, none of the three is a direct replacement for the established editors in professional film and television work today. Premiere Pro, Final Cut Pro and DaVinci Resolve support camera RAW formats, broad codec lists, plugin systems and round trips to audio and VFX departments, and Resolve and Premiere add multi-user collaboration. cinemaOS publishes no codec or RAW support list and is at version 0.2, CUTROOM exports MP4 only and is in beta, and invideo is built around uploading footage to a cloud service. For a feature film or a broadcast series with a post house, an online edit and a deliverables list, those gaps are significant.

The pressure is stronger in two other areas. The first is price. Momentum Studios builds its whole pitch on the gap between $9.99 per month and $104.99 per month for Adobe Creative Cloud Pro on the US month-to-month plan, and CUTROOM costs nothing. That argument is mainly aimed at Adobe, because DaVinci Resolve already has a free version and Final Cut Pro is available as a one-time purchase or as part of Apple Creator Studio, which costs $12.99 per month. The second area is short-form and social content, where speed counts for more than finishing depth. Vertical reframing, automatic captions, transcript-based cutting, and AI first drafts are central features in all three newcomers, and invideo adds generative shots, voices, and music on top. Creators and small marketing teams who never needed a conform or an EDL are the most likely users to switch.

The established platforms are not standing still. DaVinci Resolve 21.1 added AI assistant integration via MCP, Premiere now includes Firefly with Kling 3.0 models, and Apple has added generated captions, edit detection, and Auto Mask to Final Cut Pro. That narrows the feature gap from the other side. What the new tools show is how quickly a small team, or a single developer, can now ship an editor with a full timeline, color, sound, and AI features. ArtCraft’s FilmCraft and Cutroom are open source, so other developers can build on them. For the established vendors, the more immediate effect may be pressure on subscription pricing and on how they charge for AI, rather than a loss of their professional users.

Price and availability

cinemaOS is available now for macOS on Apple silicon at $9.99 per month excluding VAT after a 60-day free trial without a card, or $8.99 per seat per month for teams of 2 to 50 seats. CUTROOM is free and open source under the MIT license and is available as a download for Windows and Mac, with cloud AI charges paid to the user’s chosen provider. invideo’s Starter, Plus and Max plans cost $10, $30 and $75 per seat per month on annual billing, or $20, $60 and $150 on monthly billing, with 400, 2,000 and 5,000 credits per seat per month. For more information, please visit the cinemaOS, CUTROOM, and invideo websites.

Would you trust one of these new editors with a real project, or do you stay with Premiere Pro, DaVinci Resolve or Final Cut Pro? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: SmallRig Shoulder Rig Kit (Pro) vs. Classic – VCT-14 Baseplate, ARRI Rosette Arms, $419.99
entry.summary: SmallRig sells two shoulder rigs with almost the same name: the Shoulder Rig Kit (Pro) 4274B and the Shoulder Rig Kit (Classic Version) 4480B. One costs $419.99, the other $169.99, and they are built on different ideas. Here is what the extra $250 gets you, and what the Pro kit l
entry.content:
SmallRig sells two shoulder rigs with almost the same name: the Shoulder Rig Kit (Pro) 4274B and the Shoulder Rig Kit (Classic Version) 4480B. One costs $419.99, the other $169.99, and they are built on different ideas. Here is what the extra $250 gets you, and what the Pro kit leaves out of the box.

The Shoulder Rig Kit (Pro) 4274B is built around a VCT-14 shoulder pad with a silicone cushion, a two-layer quick-release plate on top, a vertically adjustable 15mm rod clamp at the front, and two retractable 1870 extension arms with ARRI rosette handles. The Shoulder Rig Kit (Classic Version) 4480B is a rod-based rig with an Arca-Swiss mount plate, a dual 15mm rod clamp, a shoulder pad, a back pad, three 15mm rods, and two handles on one rod connector. In its shoulder rig buying guide, SmallRig positions the Classic kit “for heavier builds” and the Pro kit “for more advanced cinema configurations”.

We recently had a look at a related SmallRig design at NAB 2026: the HawkLock VCT-14 Type Shoulder Rig SR009, which also uses a VCT-14 baseplate and ARRI rosette handles. The Shoulder Rig Kit (Pro) is a simpler kit, without the SR009’s back pad or sliding shoulder pad.

The differences at a glance

  • Camera mounting: the Pro kit uses a two-layer quick-release plate that slides forward and back for balance. The Classic kit uses an Arca-Swiss clamp, so a cage with a built-in Arca-Swiss plate slides straight in.
  • Tripod switch: the Pro kit has a VCT-14 baseplate under the shoulder pad. The Classic kit has 1/4″-20 and 3/8″-16 threads under the mount plate for your own quick-release plate.
  • Handles: the Pro kit uses two independent 1870 extension arms with ARRI rosettes. The Classic kit mounts both handles on one connector that clamps to the rods.
  • Body support: the Classic kit includes an adjustable back pad. The Pro kit has only the shoulder pad.
  • Rods: the Classic kit includes two 400mm and one 300mm 15mm rods. The Pro kit includes no rods.
  • Weight: 1,651g / 3.64lb for the Pro kit, 1,350g / 2.98lb for the Classic kit.

Shoulder Rig Kit (Pro): a VCT-14 plate at its core

The Pro kit consists of the VCT shoulder pad, two 1870 extension arms, and two handles. The two-layer top plate lets you shift the camera forward or back to set the center of gravity. At the front, the 15mm rod clamp moves up and down to match the rod height of different camera bodies. The extension arms retract for storage, and the silicone-covered handles rotate on their ARRI rosettes to different angles.

Under the pad sits a VCT-14 quick-release baseplate. With SmallRig’s VCT-14 Quick Release Tripod Plate 2169, which is not in the box, you can move the whole build from the shoulder to a tripod. SmallRig states that the pad is not compatible with VCT-U14 plates. The kit measures 492.3 x 203.1 x 199.9mm / 19.4 x 8.0 x 7.9in and is made of aluminum alloy, stainless steel, and silicone.

Shoulder Rig Kit (Classic Version): a lighter rod-based rig

The Classic kit uses the traditional rod layout. One knob locks the two 15mm rods in the mount plate, so you can remove the camera quickly or move the rods to change the balance. The handles sit at a 15° vertical angle, rotate through 360°, and lock with a single knob. The back pad moves forward and back to fit different operators. Both pads have 1/4″-20 threads for a V-mount battery plate or a counterweight at the rear.

SmallRig recommends a maximum load of 10kg / 22lb for the Classic kit, and gives no load rating for the Pro kit. The Classic kit measures 575.3 x 336.8 x 217.5mm / 22.6 x 13.3 x 8.6in.

Which one fits which camera?

The choice depends more on the camera than on the budget. If your camera already works with VCT-14 plates and moves between shoulder and tripod many times a day, the Pro kit fits that workflow directly. If you shoot with a mirrorless camera in a cage with an Arca-Swiss base, the Classic kit takes that cage directly, and its back pad and included rods make it a complete rig out of the box. Note that the Pro kit needs rods and a VCT-14 tripod plate at extra cost before it is a complete shoulder and tripod setup.

For more information, head to SmallRig’s site here.

Do you prefer a VCT-14 shoulder plate or a rod-based rig for your shoulder work? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: ARRI ALEXA 35 and ALEXA 265 SUP 6.2.0 Released – Full Focusbug Cine RT Integration, Shared Focus Marks, Depth of Field Ramping
entry.summary: ARRI has released Software Update Package 6.2.0 for the ALEXA 35, ALEXA 35 Xtreme, ALEXA 35 Live and ALEXA 265. The update connects the Focusbug Cine RT rangefinder directly to the camera’s SERIAL port, shares focus marks between camera and Hi-5 hand unit, and adds depth of field
entry.content:
ARRI has released Software Update Package 6.2.0 for the ALEXA 35, ALEXA 35 Xtreme, ALEXA 35 Live and ALEXA 265. The update connects the Focusbug Cine RT rangefinder directly to the camera’s SERIAL port, shares focus marks between camera and Hi-5 hand unit, and adds depth of field ramping for live productions.

SUP 6.2.0 mainly helps focus pullers, along with the multicam crews working with the ALEXA 35 Live. It also covers the 65mm ALEXA 265, which runs the same software platform.

Focusbug Cine RT without an extra box

We have previously covered the Focusbug Cine RT ultrasonic rangefinder, which reads the distance to tagged subjects. Until now, using it with an ALEXA 35 and Hi-5 required an ARRI RIA-1 radio interface adapter or an LCUBE CUB-1. With SUP 6.2.0, the camera and Hi-5 talk to the Cine RT system bi-directionally through the camera’s SERIAL port. According to ARRI, all Cine RT functions covered by the Focusbug License for Hi-5 and Hi-5 SX are now available without either adapter.

Shared focus marks

Focus marks can now be set on the camera with a programmable user button or on a connected Hi-5. Marks made on either side are synchronized automatically. They appear in the EVF and in the SDI status overlays, and the overlay can also display live distance readings from a rangefinder such as the Cine RT. ARRI notes that a new mark may appear with a delay of about one second.

Depth of field ramping for live productions

For live work, the camera can now compensate exposure automatically while the iris is adjusted. Operators can shift the depth of field between foreground and background during a broadcast while image brightness stays constant. Because this changes EI dynamically within a clip, ARRI warns that some post-production tools may ignore or misread the dynamic EI metadata, so the exposure may not be reproduced as intended. The release notes also list flicker or stepping when depth of field ramping is used with mirrored ProRes recording.

Smaller changes

Multicam SDR and HDR looks now carry an “SDR” or “HDR” prefix, so they are easier to tell apart on control panels with short character displays. A new SDI Play Mode setting lets users play back HFR clips either at project rate for slow-motion review or at the recorded frame rate.

Availability

SUP 6.2.0 is available to download now. ARRI recommends the update for all users but advises against installing it during active production. The update takes up to 20 minutes and requires a factory reset first, and the release notes list a number of known issues worth reading beforehand. For more information, please visit the ARRI website.

Will shared focus marks and direct Cine RT support change how your focus puller works with the ALEXA 35? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: Blackmagic Design Raises Prices on 36 Products – ATEM, 2110 IP Converters, and Cloud Store Hit by Memory Costs
entry.summary: Blackmagic Design has raised prices on 36 products, and the company names rising memory costs as the reason. The list covers ATEM switchers, SMPTE 2110 IP converters, DeckLink cards, HyperDeck recorders, and Cloud Store network storage, with increases from $20 to almost $7,000 pe
entry.content:
Blackmagic Design has raised prices on 36 products, and the company names rising memory costs as the reason. The list covers ATEM switchers, SMPTE 2110 IP converters, DeckLink cards, HyperDeck recorders, and Cloud Store network storage, with increases from $20 to almost $7,000 per product. Let’s take a closer look at the most recent Blackmagic price increase.

According to a company statement issued today, the new prices are effective immediately from Blackmagic Design resellers worldwide – though at the time of writing, we were still able to find the old (lower) prices at many retailers, including our partners B&H and CVP, so if you act fast (links below the article, you might still receive the goods at the old prices).

All figures about the increases mentioned below are in US dollars and exclude local duties and taxes. The price changes apply to new orders only: Blackmagic says that all current customer backorders (orders that customers have already placed but have not yet received) will be fulfilled at the original order price.

The largest single increase is on the ATEM 4 M/E Constellation IP Plus, which goes from $12,995 to $19,960 (+$6,965, or 54%). In percentage terms, the Blackmagic 2110 IP SDI to HDMI 12G sees the steepest change, from $515 to $925 (+80%). No cinema cameras are on the list.

We have previously reported on an earlier round of Blackmagic price increases that affected URSA Cine, Cloud Store, Media Modules, and ATEM products,, and on the global memory shortage behind price increases across the camera industry. Fujifilm has raised camera prices in the US, in Europe, and in Japan for the same reason, and Sony suspended orders for nearly all of its memory cards earlier this year. The movement has not been in one direction only at Blackmagic, though: in September, the company cut the prices of its full-frame 6K cameras, the Cinema Camera 6K and the PYXIS 6K.

Why Blackmagic is raising prices

In its statement, Blackmagic explains that the cost of memory (specifically the DRAM, flash, and SSD storage that “goes into almost everything we make”) has risen several times over during the past year. The company attributes this to memory manufacturers shifting their production to supply AI data centers. According to Blackmagic’s suppliers, memory consumption is now 60% higher than at the peak of the COVID shortages, and demand is a further 30% above what the suppliers can deliver. Blackmagic calculates that, in total, demand for memory is now about double what it was at the COVID peak.

The company also says why the increases come now. For some years, Blackmagic held prices down because it was building products from parts it had already bought. That stock is now being replaced with parts bought at current prices, and on the products that use a lot of memory, the company says the increase is more than it can absorb. Blackmagic names the new SMPTE 2110 products specifically, because they use much more memory. SMPTE ST 2110 is the standard for sending uncompressed video, audio, and data as separate streams over IP networks in broadcast facilities.

Blackmagic states that it is adjusting prices “only by the minimum we need to”, and that it is “still not happy about this”. The company says it will continue to search the open market for memory and other parts at better prices, pass any savings on through special deals, and return to lowering prices when parts prices come back down, which it expects to happen.

ATEM switchers take the largest increases

The ATEM line has eight products on the list, and it has the largest dollar increases of the announcement. The ATEM 4 M/E Constellation IP Plus rises from $12,995 to $19,960, and the ATEM 4 M/E Constellation IP from $7,995 to $10,845 (+$2,850). The ATEM 1 M/E Constellation 4K goes from $1,895 to $2,840 (+$945), and the ATEM 2 M/E Constellation 4K from $4,415 to $5,025 (+$610). More information on the Constellation models is available on Blackmagic’s product page.

Price and availability

The new prices are effective immediately at Blackmagic Design resellers worldwide. All prices are in US dollars and exclude local duties and taxes, so the final prices in each region will differ. Orders already placed with a reseller keep their original price. Separately, Blackmagic has also started a limited-time DaVinci Resolve Studio sale.
